echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.

New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A type of death-and-resurrection-to-life that early Christian reading connected to Christ's raising; resonates with 6:4-5,8-9 union in death and resurrection. Faint and contested.

'For they are my servants (slaves), whom I brought out of the land of Egypt' (cf. 25:55). The structural logic of 6:16-22 - one cannot be masterless; freed from one slavery you become a slave of another, and God's people are rightly God's slaves - mirrors the exodus principle that liberation from Pharaoh = transfer to YHWH's service. Coheres with Paul's 'made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness/God.'

The two ways: 'I have set before you life and death... therefore choose life.' Romans 6:21-23 frames the alternatives as 'the end of those things is death' versus 'eternal life,' the same life-or-death covenantal antithesis. Thematic coherence is high even without verbatim borrowing.

'In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die' - sin's penalty is death. 'The wages of sin is death' (6:23) restates the Edenic verdict that disobedience earns death. A foundational thematic echo behind the whole sin-death nexus of 5-6.

'You shall return to the ground... to dust you shall return' - death as the consequence of the fall. With 'wages of sin is death' (6:23) and 'the end of those things is death' (6:21) Paul echoes the Genesis sentence; note also 'the things of which you are now ashamed' (6:21) resonating with the shame of Genesis 3:7-10.
'The soul that sins shall die' (cf. 18:20). A near-proverbial scriptural maxim that sin yields death, closely cohering with 'the wages of sin is death' (6:23). Strong thematic, no formula.

The bondservant who loves his master may give himself permanently into service 'because he is well off with you' (cf. Exodus 21:5-6, serving 'forever'). Paul's voluntary, glad slavery 'obedient from the heart' (6:17) and willingly becoming 'bondservants of righteousness' (6:18) reflects this paradox of chosen, heartfelt servitude. Faint and disputed.
Circumcision of the heart so that you love and obey God; 'obedient from the heart' (6:17) echoes the prophetic-Deuteronomic ideal of interior, not merely external, obedience. Faint.

'Choose this day whom you will serve' - the demand to declare allegiance to one master. Coheres with 6:16's binary of presenting oneself as slave to sin-unto-death or to obedience-unto-righteousness. Faint, contested.

'Some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt' - the resurrection antithesis of life vs. shameful death. 'Eternal life' (6:22-23) over against death, with shame in 6:21, coheres with this Second-Temple resurrection hope. Faint and disputed.

Deuterocanonical: 'God created man for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world' (cf. 1:13, 'God did not make death'). A Second-Temple articulation that death is the intruding wage of sin, thematically close to 'the wages of sin is death' (6:23). Contested.

Deuterocanonical: 'Before a man are life and death, and whichever he chooses will be given to him'; sin and its death-penalty are laid on human choice. Coheres with the choose-your-master / death-or-life structure of 6:16,21-23. Faint and contested.
